explanation:
`std::vector` maintains its elements in contiguous memory, allowing for efficient random access (O(1)). This contiguous requirement dictates the performance characteristics of insertion and erasure operations that are not at the end.

Definition: The `vector::insert(position, element)` operation inserts a new element at a specified position. To maintain contiguous storage, all elements from `position` to the end of the vector must be shifted one position backward.

Technical Details:
- Complexity: The complexity of `insert` is linear in the number of elements that must be moved. Specifically, it is O(N - distance(begin(), position)), where N is the total size.
- Worst Case: Insertion at the beginning (`v.insert(v.begin(), x)`) requires shifting all N elements, resulting in O(N) complexity.
- Best Case: Insertion just before the end (`v.insert(v.end(), x)`) is equivalent to `push_back()` and is typically amortized O(1) (though technically O(1) if no reallocation is needed).

Usage Guidance: If frequent insertions into the middle or beginning of a sequence are required, `std::list` (O(1) insertion) or `std::deque` (O(N) worst case, but typically faster due to block structure) should be preferred over `std::vector`.

Pitfalls: Repeatedly inserting into a vector while iterating or processing data in FIFO order (inserting at the beginning) results in quadratic O(N^2) complexity, which is highly inefficient.
practical_example: When maintaining a sorted list of customer orders, inserting a new order into the middle of a `std::vector` requires linear time. If the list is large (millions of orders) and insertions are frequent, this choice leads to unacceptable performance degradation compared to using a balanced tree (`std::set`) or a linked list (`std::list`).
book: The C++ Standard Library: A Tutorial and Reference by Nicolai M. Josuttis
